lead: ls lists what exists; cat, more and less show what is inside. Every Linux user runs these commands daily to find a file, check a config, read a log, or print a page. The shell and these tools split one job: ls works on names in a directory, while the viewers work on bytes inside one file. Some syllabi call this 'listing files' and 'displaying files'. The skill is choosing the right viewer for the file size, so a 5 MiB (5,242,880 bytes) log does not flood your terminal.
prereq: You need: the one-tree view and file types from Chapter 2.1.

blocks.text: An entry is one name in a directory. ls prints entries. With no argument it lists the current directory. With a path it lists that path. A plain file name prints itself.

Options change the output. -l gives a long listing. -a includes hidden names, and also the two special entries . (current directory) and .. (parent directory). -h prints sizes as K, M, G using powers of 1024. -R lists subdirectories too. -t sorts by modification time, newest first; -r reverses the order. -i prints the inode number. -d lists the directory itself, not its contents. -F adds a slash to directories and a star to executables.

A long listing has seven fields: type and permissions, hard links, owner, group, size in bytes, date and time, name. The first character is - for a regular file, d for a directory, l for a link. The next nine characters are permissions, covered in Chapter 2.4.

The shell expands wildcards before ls runs. Typing ls *.c makes Bash replace *.c with the matching names. ls never sees the star. If nothing matches, Bash passes the pattern unchanged by default. That is why an error about a missing file named *.c can appear.

sections.h3: cat: the whole file at once

blocks.text: cat is short for concatenate. cat notes.txt copies every byte of the file to standard output. Standard output is the terminal by default. cat has no pager, so it never pauses. For a small file this is perfect: you see all lines, then your prompt returns.

cat -n notes.txt adds line numbers. cat -A notes.txt shows non-printing characters: tabs appear as ^I and line ends as $. This helps find trailing spaces. cat -s notes.txt squeezes many blank lines into one. Options combine: cat -ns notes.txt numbers lines and squeezes blanks.

On a 5 MiB log, cat big.log floods the terminal. Thousands of lines scroll past. You cannot scroll back reliably in a plain terminal, and the shell waits while it writes. Use less for large files. Relatives: tac reverses line order, head shows the first lines, and tail shows the last lines.
more and less are pagers. A pager shows one screen and waits for a key. more notes.txt moves mostly forward. Space shows the next screen. b may go back one screen in some versions. q quits.

less big.log is the stronger pager. Space moves forward, b moves back, G jumps to the last line, and g goes to the first. Type /ERROR and press Enter to search forward. Type ?ERROR and press Enter to search backward. Press n for the next match and N for the previous match. q quits.

less does not load the whole file into memory. It reads what it needs as you move. That is why it opens a huge log quickly. more is smaller but weaker; on a few systems more is a link to less, but on most distributions more is a separate, simpler program with fewer keys.
To print, lpr notes.txt sends the file to the default printer. lpq shows the print queue. Printing is different from viewing: the file leaves your terminal and waits in a queue.

figure.caption: One file can be printed whole, paged forward, paged both ways with search, or sent to a printer. Notice that cat never pauses while less can search.

examples.question: /home/ravi/lab holds notes.txt (2148 bytes), big.log (5,242,880 bytes), the hidden file .profile, and one subdirectory reports that holds two files. (a) Write the command that lists every entry, hidden ones included, with sizes in human units. How many lines does it print? (b) Write the command that lists the entry reports itself, not its contents. (c) Show notes.txt with line numbers. (d) Page through big.log, jump to the last line, then search backwards for ERROR. (e) What size does ls -lh print for big.log?
steps: (a) Use ls -lah. -a includes .profile, . and ..; -l gives long form; -h uses human sizes. Entries: ., .., .profile, big.log, notes.txt, reports = 6 entries. GNU ls also prints one total line, so GNU ls shows 7 lines; ls versions without a total line show 6.
(b) ls -ld reports. -d stops ls from opening the directory. Output is one line starting with d.
(c) cat -n notes.txt. It prints each line with a line number.
(d) less big.log. Press G to go to the last line. Type ?ERROR and press Enter to search backwards. Press n for the next match in the same direction. Press q to quit.
(e) ls -lh big.log. 5,242,880 ÷ 1024 = 5120 KiB. 5120 ÷ 1024 = 5 MiB. The size field prints 5.0M.
examples.answer: notes.txt is 2148 bytes; big.log is 5,242,880 bytes, shown as 5.0M; GNU ls -lah prints 7 lines (6 entries plus a total line), ls versions without a total line print 6, and reports holds 2 files.
examples.check:
notes = 2148
big = 5242880
mib = big / 1024 / 1024
entries = 6
files = 2
print(notes)
print(big)
print(round(mib, 1))
print(entries + 1)
print(entries)
print(files)

traps: ls -l on a directory prints the directory's contents, never the directory's own details; use -d for the entry itself.
-h divides by 1024, so 5,242,880 bytes prints as 5.0M, not 5.2M.
-a includes . and ..; -A includes hidden names but leaves out those two entries.
The shell expands *.c before ls runs. ls receives names, not the pattern.
cat -A changes only what you see on screen; it does not change the file.

quiz.q: Which option makes ls show hidden names, including . and ..?
Why does ls -l reports list files inside reports rather than one line for reports?
quiz.a: By default ls lists a directory's contents. Use -d for the directory entry itself.

quiz.q: Write a command that lists all entries with long format and human sizes, newest first.
A student runs cat big.log and the terminal becomes busy. What is the cause and a better command?
quiz.a: cat writes every byte with no paging. Use less big.log.

quiz.q: In less, which key jumps to the end, and how do you search backwards?
quiz.a: G jumps to the end; ?pattern searches backward.

quiz.q: Show notes.txt with line numbers and squeeze repeated blank lines.
In ls -li, which field is the inode, and why can two names have the same inode?
quiz.a: The first number is the inode. Two names can share one inode when they are hard links to the same file, as covered in Chapter 2.3.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pagers still sit behind man, git log, systemctl status and journalctl, so the keys you learn in less transfer directly. On servers, less +F follows a growing log like tail -f but lets you stop and search. Search next for less key bindings, the LESS environment variable, and lpq print queues.
